AI Safety Evidence Commons

For a safe future, we need a better science for AI Safety.

Improving the science of AI safety by accelerating high-quality replications.

The AI Safety Evidence Commons would improve the science of AI safety at its foundations: by re-running the findings decisions rest on, by bringing researchers in many countries and languages into that work, and by coordinating it so that effort goes where a check is missing.

Three ways to a better science of AI safety

Replication

Re-run the findings decisions rest on

A finding is a measurement taken under conditions. Re-running it with other models, prompts, judges and languages shows where it holds and where it stops. Replication is the idea underneath the whole Commons, and our AI Safety Replication Accelerator is where it starts: it keeps the repository and helps groups begin new re-runs.

  • The repository of 93 findings
  • Why replication

Global talent

Bring researchers in many countries into the work

Re-running a finding in another language needs people who speak it and know where a translated prompt goes wrong. A re-run is also a well-defined first project for a new group: the question, the method and the published answer already exist.

  • Samsekura, the first multilingual pilot
  • Offer to run a site

Coordination

Make the work add up

One shared record, common protocols, a queue of requested re-runs and a pooled fund, so that groups do not repeat each other and results from different sites can be compared.

  • 92 tools, datasets and funding sources

Why AI safety needs a better science

93findings in the repository

Decisions about which AI systems are safe to build and release rest on a small number of experiments. Governments are asked to act on that evidence before it is settled.

The International AI Safety Report 2026 calls this an “evidence dilemma”.

65of 93 tested in English alone

Most of those experiments were run once, by the team that made them, on particular models, prompts, judges and languages. The conditions drop out as a finding is cited.

As Niederman asks: where are the AI safety replications?

17of 56 held in full when others re-ran them

When someone else re-runs a finding, the result often narrows. Sciences learn which results hold by re-running them. In AI safety that is still rare and slow.

As Roe argues, influential papers are usually true in some sense but incomplete.

The full case, with sources

Fewer than a third of the re-tested findings in the repository held in full.

Each seed is one of the 93 findings in the repository, placed by year of publication. Each shoot is one of 184 later re-runs and follow-up studies, ending in a leaf coloured by what it found. The 37 hollow seeds have no independent re-run found; for 23 of them the search was cut short, so some may exist. Select a seed to open its record, or see the same findings as a sortable list.

ReplicatedPartly replicatedConditionalContested or did not replicateFollow-up or extensionNo independent re-run found

Anyone who runs, funds or relies on these findings can take part.

  • Re-run a study

    Of the 93 findings, 66 could be re-run for under about $500 in compute. Choose one and register it, so others can see it is underway.

  • Offer to run a site

    Groups that can run a shared protocol in their language could join Samsekura’s pilot or a later round.

  • Request a replication

    Name a finding and the decision its result would inform.

  • Fund the pool, or use the data

    A pooled fund would pay for re-runs on publication, whatever they show. The repository is free to download.
